title: The Erdős number
hook: Mathematicians still count how many steps they are from one wandering man.
peek: Paul Erdős wrote around 1,500 papers with more than 500 co-authors, travelling with little more than a suitcase. Mathematicians honour him with a number: 1 if you wrote a paper with him, 2 if you wrote with one of his co-authors, and so on.
lede: Paul Erdős, a Hungarian mathematician who lived from 1913 to 1996, had no fixed home for much of his life. He travelled from one university to the next with a half-empty suitcase, staying with colleagues and working on problems with them. He wrote around 1,500 papers with more than 500 co-authors, so many that mathematicians began measuring their distance from him.

bullets.text: Erdős himself has Erdős number 0. Anyone who wrote a paper with him has 1, their co-authors who did not have 2, and so on. People with no chain of co-authors back to him have an infinite Erdős number.
Researchers at Oakland University track the collaboration network. They have found that most working mathematicians are only a few steps away, with a typical Erdős number of about 5.
Erdős offered his own money for solutions to problems he posed, from a few dollars up to thousands. Some winners framed his cheques instead of cashing them.
Erdős loved to repeat that a mathematician is a machine for turning coffee into theorems. The line is usually credited to him, but it seems to have come from his friend and collaborator Alfréd Rényi.

A playful extension adds your Erdős number to your Bacon number, the steps to the actor Kevin Bacon through shared films. A few people, including some actors who have co-written science papers, have a finite score.
